sentences.english_text: When they reached the ground, the young man handed the box to the priest.
A cheer went up from the crowd.
They all pressed forward to take a look at the tear of the saint's statue.
But the priest held them back.
I will take it to the church.
You may all come and look at it.
And the priest started toward the church carrying the box, the crowd following him.
When they reached the church, the priest walked to the altar and carefully set the box down.
The people walked past single file, each one stopping to look down at Drippy, who by now was sound asleep from his hard day's activities.
It's beautiful.
You can tell it's a miracle.
I've never seen such a lovely tear.
And so it went.
Hundreds and hundreds of people passed by the altar, looking down at Drippy, innocently sleeping in the little box.
And each of them believed that they were looking at a miracle.
In a way, of course, they were right.
For raindrops are miracles.
But then isn't every form of life really a miracle?
When the last of the people had gone, the priest locked up the church and went home, leaving Drippy asleep on the altar.
Tomorrow, the teardrop will be on its way to Rome.
But the priest was wrong.
At midnight, when everyone was in bed asleep, a man broke into the church to steal the miracle.
If it's worth so much to the church, then let them pay for it.
I'll sell it back to them.
He crept over to the altar and carefully shook Drippy out of the little box he was in, into a small iron box.
The fall made Drippy wake up.
He saw what was happening, but before he could say a word, an iron lid slammed down over his head.
Drippy was being kidnapped.
